title: Federal Government Shutdown Stalls Disaster Readiness, Leaves California at Risk, Newsom Says - NewsBreak
text:
4 hours ago SACRAMENTO – California officials are warning that the ongoing federal government shutdown under Donald Trump is threatening the state’s ability to prepare for and recover from disasters. Governor Gavin Newsom said the freeze on federal disaster programs and furloughs of critical staff are leaving communities across California more vulnerable as fire season looms.
Photo by Louis Velazquez on Unsplash “As of this morning, the Trump government shutdown has forced thousands of critical federal employees in California onto furlough and put key disaster recovery programs on pause,” Newsom said. “Wildfire crews and emergency responders remain on the front lines, but federal support for community preparedness, forest management and prescribed fires, and recovery grants is now frozen.”
The governor underscored the danger in blunt terms. “Communities across our state are less safe because of Trump’s government shutdown. Thanks to Donald Trump, critical wildfire preparedness and disaster recovery programs are on pause. This can’t go on – Republicans need to act to end this shutdown,” Newsom said.
In Sacramento, state officials confirmed that FEMA field staff remain active, but reimbursements and mitigation funding are stalled. The National Weather Service is still issuing warnings, but climate research and upgrades are suspended, delaying long-term prevention. In California’s national parks, more than two-thirds of federal staff are furloughed, leaving limited emergency coverage for fires, rescues, and visitor safety.
Despite the gridlock in Washington, California agencies remain fully staffed. CAL FIRE, Cal OES, CHP, and the California National Guard continue to operate, with CAL FIRE having expanded its workforce by thousands in recent years. Since 2019, the state has invested more than $5 billion in wildfire prevention and resilience, including $135 million for new projects and 103 vegetation management efforts covering 25,000 acres.
California’s investments stand in sharp contrast to federal cuts. State officials say Trump’s reductions to the U.S. Forest Service—eliminating 10% of positions and furloughing a quarter of prevention staff—are compounding the risks. The proposed closure of regional Forest Service offices across the West would further weaken disaster readiness just as California faces historic fire threats.
